title: When Bolivia's Microlender PRODEM Turned Itself Into a Bank
dek: In 1992 the leaders of a fast-growing Bolivian non-profit chose to move its lending into a regulated commercial bank, BancoSol, despite fears it would lose its purpose.

story.founder: Francisco (Pancho) Otero, with PRODEM's founding partners
story.event: Moving a microfinance NGO's loan book into a new commercial bank, Banco Solidario
story.summary: PRODEM, a Bolivian microlending NGO set up in 1986 with ACCION International and led by Pancho Otero, grew so fast on donor funds that by 1990 its leaders believed non-profit status was limiting it. In February 1992 it transferred a $3.96 million portfolio and about 14,300 active clients to Banco Solidario (BancoSol), a regulated commercial bank owned mainly by NGOs and donors with prominent Bolivian investors; the bank grew rapidly, took deposits, and later survived the sacking of its branches in 2003.
paragraphs: In 1986 ACCION International hired Francisco Otero, known as Pancho, to start a lending organisation for Bolivia's microentrepreneurs. The result, PRODEM, was a non-profit backed by Bolivian business leaders and grants from USAID and the Inter-American Development Bank. From 1987 it lent small sums to self-employed people and family businesses in Bolivia's cities, often through solidarity groups whose members stood behind one another's loans. Elisabeth Rhyne, who knew him, later called Otero a "radical anti-banker".

PRODEM grew faster than expected, and by 1990 its leaders believed non-profit status was holding it back. Its lending money came from donors, on donors' terms; it could not take deposits or borrow from banks to meet the seasonal swings in clients' needs. Ohio State researchers later wrote that being unable to grow as they wished frustrated PRODEM's leaders. They also knew the model worked: repayment was strong, and PRODEM had cut its reliance on subsidy sharply by lowering costs rather than raising rates.

The choice was to split. PRODEM would stay a foundation, and a new private commercial bank, Banco Solidario, would take over its urban lending under the bank supervisor's full prudential rules. By a later chief executive's account, the vote divided directors and investors, some of whom feared a bank would lose sight of its social purpose. Shareholders included ACCION, the Calmeadow and Rockefeller foundations, PRODEM itself, three Bolivian banks and five prominent Bolivians, among them Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada, later president; researchers wrote that the charter was granted on their reputations. In February 1992 PRODEM handed BancoSol a $3.96 million loan portfolio and about 14,300 active clients, and Otero became its first chief executive.

Now able to take deposits and borrow, the bank grew fast: from 1992 to 1994 its portfolio rose tenfold in real terms and active borrowers passed 60,000. PRODEM's founding team was joined by professional bankers, and the debates between the two camps were, the researchers noted, intense. PRODEM itself turned to rural lending.

The doubts did not vanish. In 2003, amid national unrest and anger over borrowers' debts, crowds sacked BancoSol branches in La Paz and El Alto. The bank recovered, and around 2011 Rhyne counted nearly 150,000 borrowers and 440,000 savers.

quote.text: One is the road that leads to wealth, another the road that leads to Nirvana
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The Dhammapada keeps the road to wealth and the road to release apart. BancoSol's founders bet that for their clients a profitable bank was the surest road to wider reach, while some of their own directors feared the roads would part. The sacked branches of 2003 did not settle the argument.

reflection: Some of PRODEM's own directors feared a bank would forget why it existed. The fear was reasonable, and it did not go away: researchers checked for mission drift in 1996, and protesters asked the same question far more harshly in 2003. Changing the form of the work did not end the argument about its purpose; it carried the argument into new rooms.

You may meet a version of this: a grant that ends, a buyer who wants something more commercial, a new way your work is paid for. The worry that you will lose what matters is not a reason to refuse the change. It is worth keeping near, because it often notices drift before anyone else does.
invitation: Write one sentence naming what your work must keep doing whatever form it takes. Show it to one colleague today and ask whether they would recognise your work in it.

cross_checks.claim: PRODEM was a non-profit started in the mid-1980s with ACCION International, and Pancho Otero led it and became BancoSol's first chief executive.
PRODEM's leaders concluded that NGO status and dependence on donor funds limited its growth, and created a commercial bank in 1992.
The decision raised fears that the bank would lose its social mission.
Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada was among the founders of PRODEM and an original shareholder in BancoSol.
BancoSol grew rapidly after 1992 by mobilising deposits and commercial funds.

research_notes: Size of the transferred book disagrees: the Ohio State study (1996, citing Agafonoff 1994) says PRODEM transferred a $3.96 million portfolio with about 14,300 active clients in February 1992 (eventually $6.48 million once more branches moved); World Finance, drawing on BancoSol's later account, says PRODEM had about 17,000 clients and $4 million in loans after six years. The story uses the study's dated figures. Founding dates: World Finance and MicroSave give 1986 for PRODEM's founding and Otero's hiring; the Ohio State study says PRODEM began operations in 1987; the story uses both in that sense. Who founded PRODEM varies by source (ACCION with Bolivian business leaders; ACCION with USAID and IDB grants; Bolivian entrepreneurs with international backers), so the story names ACCION, Bolivian business leaders and the grant-makers without ranking them. The Ohio State study notes that the USAID mission had substantial funds for PRODEM and wanted fast growth, so the story describes donor money as inflexible rather than scarce. The account of the divided vote comes from Kurt Koenigsfest, a later chief executive, in World Finance, and is attributed to him; the exact date of the vote is not documented in the sources used. Otero's own voice is available only in summary (MicroSave's 2011 video page), so the story quotes Rhyne's description of him instead. Rhyne's ReVista essay looks back from about 2011 (posted on the web in 2021); its client figures are dated accordingly. The causes of the 2003 attacks are given as Rhyne put them (over-indebtedness after a rush to lend, and wider political anger), without assigning blame. The Dhammapada verse is addressed to a disciple renouncing the world; it is applied by analogy to the argument over mission and profit.
